title: How Did Daylight Saving Time Start?
question: How did daylight saving time start, and why can't we stop changing the clocks?
description: Clocks across America fell back this weekend, months after the House voted to make daylight saving time permanent. So how did the world end up changing its clocks twice a year? From Benjamin Franklin's joke and a New Zealand bug collector to a London builder and the First World War, here's how daylight saving time began, what it really saves, and why it's so hard to stop. Lighter mornings or lighter evenings: which would you keep?

ad_safety.reason: History and policy explainer; both sides of the current debate presented.

scenes.narration: Last night, clocks across America fell back an hour. Most of Europe did the same a week earlier.

visual.text: How did daylight saving time start?

scenes.narration: And this year, it nearly didn't happen. In July, the US House of Representatives voted to make daylight saving time permanent.

visual.label: House vote to make daylight saving time permanent, July 2026

scenes.narration: So how did so much of the world end up moving its clocks twice a year? And why is it so hard to stop?

visual.text: Why do we change the clocks at all?

sections.heading: A joke and a bug collector

scenes.narration: The story usually starts with Benjamin Franklin. In 1784, living in Paris, he wrote a letter to a newspaper about the cost of candles.

visual.label: Benjamin Franklin, 1784
visual.sub: A letter to the Journal de Paris

scenes.narration: His plan? Tax every window shutter, ration candles, and ring church bells, or even fire cannons, at sunrise to get people out of bed.

items.text: Ring bells, fire cannons at dawn

scenes.narration: It was a joke. Franklin never suggested changing the clocks at all.
The first serious proposal came in 1895, from George Hudson, a New Zealand insect collector who wanted more daylight after work to hunt for bugs.
He suggested moving the clocks forward by two whole hours in summer. Hardly anyone took him seriously.
Then came William Willett, a London builder. Out riding early one summer morning, he noticed how many houses still had their blinds down.

visual.label: William Willett
visual.sub: A London builder who hated wasted mornings

scenes.narration: In 1907, he paid to publish a pamphlet with a blunt title: The Waste of Daylight.
His plan was oddly precise. Move the clocks forward eighty minutes in April, in four steps of twenty minutes, then back again in September.
He spent years lobbying Parliament. It never became law in his lifetime. Willett died in 1915.
A year later, war did what campaigning couldn't.
On the thirtieth of April, 1916, Germany and Austria-Hungary put their clocks forward, to save coal for the war effort.
Lighter evenings meant fewer lamps lit, and fewer lamps meant less coal burned. Coal was what the war ran on.
Britain followed within weeks. Parliament passed the bill on the seventeenth of May, and the clocks went forward four days later.
The United States joined in 1918, then scrapped it nationally straight after the war, after strong opposition, especially from farmers.
For decades after that, American cities and states set their own rules, and the time could change from one town to the next.

visual.label: A patchwork of clocks
visual.sub: Cities and states set their own rules

scenes.narration: In 1966, the Uniform Time Act brought order: one national schedule, though states were allowed to opt out.

visual.label: Uniform Time Act, 1966
visual.sub: One schedule. States may opt out.

scenes.narration: That's why Hawaii and most of Arizona never change their clocks at all.

items.text: Most of Arizona: no clock changes

scenes.narration: In 1974, during an oil crisis, America even tried daylight saving time all year round.

visual.label: 1974: all year round
visual.sub: An experiment during the oil crisis

scenes.narration: It was popular, until winter came and children were walking to school in the dark. Congress ended the experiment early, that October.
So does changing the clocks actually save energy? That was always the promise.
When America lengthened daylight saving time in 2007, the Department of Energy measured what happened.
It found a saving of about half a percent of electricity on each extra day. Across the whole year, that came to about three hundredths of one percent.

visual.title: Electricity saved by the longer daylight saving period

scenes.narration: A real saving, but a tiny one.
Sleep doctors say the switch itself has a cost, because your body runs on its own clock.
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says traffic deaths rise by as much as six percent in the first few days after clocks spring forward.

visual.label: rise in traffic deaths in the days after the spring change

scenes.narration: So the academy wants the changes to stop, and standard time kept all year, because morning light keeps the body clock in step.
Here's the catch. Most people want the changing to stop. They just can't agree which time to keep.
The House bill picks daylight time. Supporters, including President Trump, want more light in the evening, after work and school.

visual.label: For: lighter evenings
visual.sub: More daylight after work and school

scenes.narration: Critics in the Senate warn that in parts of the country, winter sunrise would come after nine in the morning, with children heading to school in the dark.

visual.label: Against: dark mornings
visual.sub: Winter sunrise after 9am in some places

scenes.narration: As of this weekend, the bill is stuck in the Senate. So the clocks changed again.

visual.label: Stuck in the Senate
visual.sub: So the clocks fell back again

scenes.narration: America isn't alone. Seventy countries still change their clocks, and seventy three others tried it, then gave up.
In 2019, the European Parliament voted to end clock changes too. But Europe still changes them, because countries couldn't agree on which time to keep.

visual.label: Voted to stop in 2019. Still changing.

scenes.narration: And near the equator, most countries never bothered. Daylight there barely changes through the year.

visual.label: Near the equator
visual.sub: Days stay close to 12 hours all year

scenes.narration: So daylight saving time began as a joke, became a bug collector's dream, a builder's crusade, and then a wartime way to save coal.
More than a century later, we're still changing the clocks, mostly because we can't agree on how to stop.

visual.text: We still can't agree how to stop.

scenes.narration: So which would you keep: lighter mornings, or lighter evenings? Tell us in the comments.

short.outro: That's how daylight saving time started. The full story is on Every How.
